about: NORTHUMBRIA, DANISH YORK AND THE NORTHERN EARLDOMS, 780-1070: who rules, the wars, the raids, the laws, the coins and the church, so the game can say who holds York and Bamburgh in any year and what that means for a ship in the Humber or off the Tyne. Realm id 'northumbria' (ports eoforwic, lindisfarena, bebbanburg, gyrwe, streonaeshalch). Every ruler has 'part': all (the whole kingdom or earldom), york (south of the Tees: the Danish kingdom, then the earldom of York), bamburgh (north of the Tees or Tyne: the English lords of Bamburgh), overlord (a southern king who holds the north through others). To ask who rules a place in a year, take the entries whose part is that place's part or 'all' and whose from-to holds the year; the overlord is extra. Years are whole years AD; days are in the text. 'seat' and 'where' are port ids from ports_793.json where the place is one, else a plain place name. (?) marks a doubt or a fact not re-checked. 'certainty' on raids is sure / likely / uncertain, as in chronicle_793.json; 'chronicle' gives the id of the matching entry there, where there is one. 'by_realm' true marks a raid made out of this realm on others. Sources are named as chronicle_793.json names them; quoted words of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle are Ingram 1823, of the laws Thorpe 1840. Written 4 October 2026. Edit freely.

rulers.name: Ælfwald I
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Murdered on 23 September 788 by his ealdorman Sicga at Scythlecester near the Wall; buried at Hexham.

rulers.name: Osred II
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Betrayed by his nobles, tonsured at York and driven out to the Isle of Man. He came back in 792, was taken and killed on 14 September and buried at Tynemouth.

rulers.name: Æthelred I (second reign)
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Killed by his own nobles on 18 April 796 at Corbridge.
rulers.note: In 791 he had Ælfwald's two sons coaxed out of York minster and drowned. On 29 September 792 he married Ælfflæd, daughter of Offa of Mercia, at Catterick. He is the king of the Lindisfarne year.

rulers.name: Osbald
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Deserted after 27 days, he fled to Lindisfarne and sailed with some of the brothers to the king of the Picts. He died an abbot in 799 and was buried at York.

rulers.name: Eardwulf
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Driven out of the kingdom (the Chronicle says 806; the Frankish annals have him arrive at Nijmegen in Lent 808).
rulers.note: Made king on 14 May 796 and hallowed at York on 26 May. About 790, as a young ealdorman, he was put to death outside the gate of Ripon on Æthelred's order; the monks laid the body by the church, and after midnight he was found alive inside it.

rulers.name: Ælfwald II
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Gave way when Eardwulf was brought back; nothing more is told of him.
rulers.source: ASC (D/E) 806; LDE ii.5 (two years); RW 808; num.: stycas by the moneyer Cuthheard

rulers.name: Eardwulf (restored)
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded. His son Eanred follows about 810 (?).
rulers.note: Led home in late 808 by the pope's deacon Aldulf and the emperor's abbots Hruotfrid and Nanthar: the only English king put back by Frankish and Roman envoys.
rulers.source: ARF 808, 809; Leo III, letters to Charles (808)

rulers.name: Eanred
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Died, about 840 or 841. Some who study the coins would put his whole reign later, to about 850 (?).
rulers.note: Thirty years with no recorded raid and no recorded killing of a king: the quiet time. In 829 he met Ecgberht of Wessex at Dore and offered obedience.

rulers.name: Æthelred II
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Driven out by Rædwulf.

rulers.name: Rædwulf
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Killed within the year fighting heathen raiders at a place written Alutthelia (unknown), with Ealdorman Alfred and many of his men.
rulers.source: RW 844; num.: his stycas prove the reign

rulers.name: Æthelred II (restored)
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Killed, in 848 or 849; no more is told.

rulers.name: Osberht
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Driven out by Ælla about 862 or 863 (the Chronicle makes it shortly before 867 (?)). Made peace with him in 867 and was killed with him at York on 21 March.
rulers.note: The Cuthbert tradition says he took Warkworth and Tillmouth from the saint, and paid for it.

rulers.name: Ælla
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians, not of the royal kin
rulers.how_ended: Killed at York on 21 March 867 when he and Osberht broke into the city against the great army.
rulers.note: The Chronicle calls him a king 'not of the kin'. The snake-pit of Ragnar and the blood-eagle are later saga stories, not history (?).

rulers.name: Ecgberht I
rulers.title: king under the great army
rulers.how_ended: Driven out by the Northumbrians in 872, together with Archbishop Wulfhere; died in 873.
rulers.note: Set up by the army of Ivar and Halfdan, which itself lay at York in 866-867 and again for a year in 868-869. The Durham writers say he ruled 'beyond the Tyne'; at York the army's word was the law.

rulers.name: Ricsige
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Died in 876, the year Halfdan shared out the land.

rulers.name: Halfdan
rulers.title: king of the army in Northumbria
rulers.how_ended: Driven out by his own army (the Cuthbert tradition says he went mad and stank, and left the Tyne with three ships); killed in Ireland at Strangford Lough in 877.
rulers.note: Wintered on the Tyne in 874-875 and raided the Picts and the Strathclyde Britons; in 876 he shared out the land of the Northumbrians and his men began to plough.

rulers.name: Ecgberht II
rulers.title: king of the Northumbrians beyond the Tyne
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded; the Durham annals give him two years (?).

rulers.name: (no king known at York)
rulers.title: the army without a king
rulers.how_ended: Ended when the army and the English together took Guthred as king.

rulers.name: Eadwulf of Bamburgh
rulers.title: lord of Bamburgh; 'king of the northern Saxons' in the Irish annals
rulers.how_ended: Died in 913.
rulers.note: When he began is not known (?); he was a friend of King Alfred. His house holds Bamburgh, with breaks, until 1067.

rulers.name: Guthred (Guthfrith) son of Harthacnut
rulers.title: king at York, a Christian Dane
rulers.how_ended: Died on 24 August 895 (the feast of Saint Bartholomew) and was buried in York minster.
rulers.note: A boy sold as a slave to a widow at Whittingham, bought free and made king on the hill called Oswigesdune with a gold ring on his right arm, at the word of Abbot Eadred of Carlisle, who said Saint Cuthbert had told him so in a dream.

rulers.name: Siefred (Sigeferth)
rulers.title: king at York
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded: he is known from his pennies. He may be the Sigeferth who led a fleet out of Northumbria against the south in 893 (?).
rulers.source: num.: the Cuerdale hoard (Blackburn 2004); Æthelweard iv.3

rulers.name: Æthelwold ætheling
rulers.title: a West Saxon prince taken as king by the army in Northumbria
rulers.how_ended: Sailed south with a fleet to Essex and was killed at the battle of the Holme, December 902.
rulers.source: ASC (A) 900 (=899); ASC (A, D) 904-905 (=902); num.: pennies reading ALVALDVS

rulers.name: Cnut
rulers.title: king at York
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded: he is known only from his pennies, some three thousand of them in the Cuerdale hoard.

rulers.name: Halfdan, Eowils and Ivar
rulers.title: kings of the army in Northumbria
rulers.how_ended: All killed at Tettenhall on 5 August 910, coming home from a raid deep into Mercia.

rulers.name: (no king known at York)
rulers.title: the men of York
rulers.how_ended: Ended when Ragnall stormed the city in 919.
rulers.note: The Saint Peter pennies carry no king's name in these years. In 918 the people of York promised, some by pledge and some by oath, to put themselves under Æthelflæd of Mercia; she died on 12 June before it came to anything.

rulers.name: Ealdred son of Eadwulf
rulers.title: lord of Bamburgh
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded; last seen about 933 (?). The Irish annals have an 'Adulf son of Eadwulf, king of the northern Saxons' die in 934, who may be the same man or his brother (?).
rulers.note: Driven out by Ragnall about 914 and fled to Constantine of the Scots; back by 920, when 'the sons of Eadwulf' took King Edward as lord; bowed to Æthelstan at Eamont in 927.
rulers.source: HSC 22; ASC (A) 920; ASC (D) 926 (=927); Annals of Clonmacnoise 934 (?)

rulers.name: Ragnall, grandson of Ivar
rulers.title: king at York; 'king of the fair foreigners and the dark foreigners' in the Irish annals
rulers.how_ended: Died in 921.
rulers.note: Came by sea from the Irish Sea, beat the Scots and the Bamburgh English on the Tyne at Corbridge (918), gave Saint Cuthbert's lands to his men Scula and Onlafbald, and took York in 919. In 920 he took King Edward as lord.

rulers.name: Sihtric, grandson of Ivar
rulers.title: king at York
rulers.how_ended: Died in 927.
rulers.note: Came from Dublin. Met Æthelstan at Tamworth on 30 January 926 and married his sister; a later writer says he soon put away both her and the faith (?).

rulers.name: Guthfrith, grandson of Ivar
rulers.title: king at York
rulers.how_ended: Came from Dublin for his kinsman's kingdom and was driven out by Æthelstan within months.

rulers.name: Æthelstan
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Died at Gloucester on 27 October 939.
rulers.note: The first southern king to hold York. He pulled down the stronghold the Danes had built in the city and shared out what was in it. His own seat is in the south; York is kept by his reeves and the archbishop.

rulers.name: Oswulf of Bamburgh
rulers.title: high-reeve of Bamburgh
rulers.how_ended: Became earl of all Northumbria in 954 (see his second entry).
rulers.source: charters of the 930s to 950s; RW 950; DPSA

rulers.name: Olaf Guthfrithson
rulers.title: king at York and at Dublin
rulers.how_ended: Died in 941, soon after burning the church of Saint Balthere at Tyninghame.
rulers.note: The loser at Brunanburh in 937. Taken as king at York within weeks of Æthelstan's death; in 940, by a peace the two archbishops made, his kingdom reached south to Watling Street.

rulers.name: Olaf Sihtricson (Cuaran)
rulers.title: king at York
rulers.how_ended: Driven out: the Durham annals say by the Northumbrians in 943 (?), the Chronicle by King Edmund in 944.
rulers.note: Baptised in 943 with King Edmund as his godfather.

rulers.name: Ragnall Guthfrithson
rulers.title: king at York
rulers.how_ended: Driven out by King Edmund in 944.
rulers.note: Whether he shared the kingdom with Olaf or was set up against him is not known.

rulers.name: Edmund
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Stabbed at Pucklechurch on 26 May 946.

rulers.name: Eadred
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: In 947 Archbishop Wulfstan and the Northumbrian council swore to him at Tanshelf, and soon broke it and took Eric as king.

rulers.name: Eric son of Harald
rulers.title: king at York
rulers.how_ended: Given up by the Northumbrians in 948 when Eadred threatened to waste the whole land; they paid the king for the wrong.
rulers.note: The later sagas make him Eric Bloodaxe, son of Harald Fairhair, driven out of Norway; some doubt it (?).

rulers.name: Eadred (again)
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Olaf came back to Northumbria in 949.

rulers.name: Olaf Sihtricson (second reign)
rulers.title: king at York
rulers.how_ended: Driven out by the Northumbrians in 952; he went back to rule Dublin until 980.

rulers.name: Eric son of Harald (second reign)
rulers.title: king at York, the last
rulers.how_ended: Driven out by the Northumbrians in 954 and killed on Stainmore by Maccus son of Olaf, betrayed by Oswulf of Bamburgh, with his son and his brother.

rulers.name: Oswulf of Bamburgh
rulers.title: earl of all the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded (last seen about 963 to 966); after him the earldom is split at the Tees, or the Tyne.
rulers.note: From 954 there are no more kings in the north: the king of the English rules it through earls.

rulers.name: Oslac
rulers.title: earl at York
rulers.how_ended: Banished over the sea in 975, after King Edgar's death.

rulers.name: Eadwulf Evil-child
rulers.title: earl from the Tees to Myreforth
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded (?).
rulers.note: Said to have led Kenneth of the Scots to King Edgar with Oslac and the bishop, about 973, when Kenneth was given Lothian (?).

rulers.name: Thored
rulers.title: earl at York
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded; last named in 992, as one of the leaders of the king's fleet that failed.
rulers.note: Perhaps the Thored son of Gunnar who harried Westmorland in 966. His daughter Ælfgifu married King Æthelred.

rulers.name: Waltheof
rulers.title: earl at Bamburgh
rulers.how_ended: Too old to fight when the Scots came in 1006, he shut himself in Bamburgh; the king gave his earldom to his son Uhtred.

rulers.name: Ælfhelm
rulers.title: earl at York, a Mercian
rulers.how_ended: Murdered in 1006 (John of Worcester: by Eadric Streona, at a hunt near Shrewsbury); his sons Wulfheah and Ufegeat were blinded.
rulers.note: His daughter Ælfgifu of Northampton was later Cnut's wife in the Danish manner.

rulers.name: Uhtred
rulers.title: earl of all the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Came to Cnut at Wiheal in 1016 to give hostages and was cut down in the hall with forty of his men by Thurbrand, called the Hold, whose men had hidden behind a curtain.
rulers.note: He beat the Scots at Durham in 1006, bowed to Sweyn in 1013 and went back to Æthelred, whose daughter he married. His killing began a feud of four generations.

rulers.name: Eric of Hlathir
rulers.title: earl at York, a Norwegian
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded; he last witnesses a charter in 1023.
rulers.note: Eiríkr Hákonarson, Cnut's brother-in-law, who had fought at Svolder.

rulers.name: Eadwulf Cudel
rulers.title: earl at Bamburgh
rulers.how_ended: Died within a few years (?).
rulers.note: Uhtred's brother; 'a lazy and cowardly man' to the Durham writer, who says he gave up Lothian to the Scots for fear. The English lost at Carham on the Tweed in 1018.

rulers.name: Ealdred son of Uhtred
rulers.title: earl at Bamburgh
rulers.how_ended: Killed in the wood called Risewood by Carl son of Thurbrand, about 1038 (?).
rulers.note: He had killed Thurbrand for his father. He and Carl were made friends and meant to go to Rome together, were kept in harbour by a storm, and Carl killed him on the way home.

rulers.name: (earl not known)
rulers.title: earl at York
rulers.how_ended: Siward is first named as earl in 1033.
rulers.note: Carl son of Thurbrand is the great man at York in these years (?).

rulers.name: Siward
rulers.title: earl at York, a Dane
rulers.how_ended: Died at York in 1055 and was buried at Galmanho in the church he had built and had hallowed in the name of God and Olaf.
rulers.note: From 1041 he held Bamburgh too. In 1054 he beat Macbeth. A later tale says that, dying of the flux, he had himself armed so as not to die like a cow.
rulers.source: ASC (C/D) 1054, 1055; LDE iii.9; Henry of Huntingdon vi (?)

rulers.name: Eadwulf son of Uhtred
rulers.title: earl at Bamburgh
rulers.how_ended: Came to King Harthacnut under safe-conduct in 1041 and was killed by Siward.
rulers.note: Harried the Britons (of Cumbria) in 1038.

rulers.name: Siward
rulers.title: earl of all the Northumbrians
rulers.how_ended: Died at York in 1055.
rulers.note: He married Ælfflæd, Earl Ealdred's daughter, and so joined the two houses.

rulers.name: Tostig son of Godwine
rulers.title: earl of all the Northumbrians, a West Saxon
rulers.how_ended: On 3 October 1065 the thegns of the north took York, killed his housecarls, broke open his treasury and outlawed him; the king gave way at Oxford on 28 October and Tostig crossed to Flanders.
rulers.note: The first earl from the south. He put down robbers hard, taxed heavily, and had Gamal son of Orm and Ulf son of Dolfin killed in his own chamber at York under a promise of peace (1064). Copsi ruled under him.

rulers.name: Morcar son of Ælfgar
rulers.title: earl of all the Northumbrians, a Mercian
rulers.how_ended: Beaten at Fulford (20 September 1066); bowed to William; joined the rising of 1068 and lost the north. Taken at Ely in 1071 and kept a prisoner.
rulers.note: He gave the land beyond the Tyne to Oswulf son of Eadwulf.

rulers.name: Oswulf son of Eadwulf
rulers.title: earl beyond the Tyne
rulers.how_ended: Run through by a robber's spear in the autumn of 1067.
rulers.note: Put out by King William for Copsi in early 1067, he took to the hills, came back and killed him, and held the earldom till the autumn.

rulers.name: Copsi
rulers.title: earl beyond the Tyne by King William's gift
rulers.how_ended: Killed at Newburn on the Tyne on 12 March 1067, in the fifth week of his earldom: Oswulf fired the church he had fled into and cut him down at the door.

rulers.name: Gospatric son of Maldred
rulers.title: earl beyond the Tyne
rulers.how_ended: Bought the earldom from King William at Christmas 1067 for a great sum; joined the rising of 1068 and fled to Scotland.

rulers.name: William Malet
rulers.title: the king's sheriff at York, keeper of the castle
rulers.how_ended: Taken alive with his wife and two children when the Danes and the English stormed the castles on 21 September 1069.

rulers.name: Robert de Comines
rulers.title: earl beyond the Tees by King William's gift
rulers.how_ended: Killed at Durham at dawn on 28 January 1069, the night after he came, with all his men but one or two (700 by Symeon, 900 by the Chronicle); the bishop's house was burned over him.

rulers.name: King William in person
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: He kept Christmas 1069 in the burnt city and wasted the land from the Humber to the Tees and beyond; in 1070 he gave the see to Thomas of Bayeux and went south.

rulers.name: Gospatric son of Maldred (restored)
rulers.title: earl beyond the Tyne
rulers.how_ended: Submitted to William by messengers on the Tees in January 1070 and was given the earldom back; deprived in 1072.

rulers.name: Eadred
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Died 23 November 955.

rulers.name: Eadwig
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: In 957 the Mercians and Northumbrians took his brother Edgar as king north of the Thames.

rulers.name: Edgar
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Died 8 July 975.

rulers.name: Edward (the Martyr)
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Murdered at Corfe, 18 March 978.

rulers.name: Æthelred II
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Fled to Normandy at Christmas 1013; the north had bowed to Sweyn at Gainsborough that summer.

rulers.name: Sweyn Forkbeard
rulers.title: king of the Danes, taken as king by the north
rulers.how_ended: Died at Gainsborough on 3 February 1014.

rulers.name: Æthelred II (again)
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Died in London on 23 April 1016. The north had already gone over to Cnut that spring.

rulers.name: Cnut
rulers.title: king of the English, later also of the Danes and Norwegians
rulers.how_ended: Died at Shaftesbury on 12 November 1035.

rulers.name: Harold Harefoot
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Died at Oxford on 17 March 1040.

rulers.name: Harthacnut
rulers.title: king of the English and the Danes
rulers.how_ended: Died at Lambeth on 8 June 1042.

rulers.name: Edward (the Confessor)
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Died at Westminster on 5 January 1066.

rulers.name: Harold son of Godwine
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Killed at Hastings on 14 October 1066, nineteen days after Stamford Bridge.
rulers.note: He came to York about Easter 1066 to win the north over (?).
rulers.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1066; William of Malmesbury, Vita Wulfstani i.16 (?)

rulers.name: William
rulers.title: king of the English, duke of the Normans
rulers.seat: the south; castles at eoforwic from 1068
rulers.how_ended: Died at Rouen on 9 September 1087, after the span of this file.

wars.who: the Northumbrian royal kins against each other: Ælfwald I, Osred II, Æthelred I, Osbald, Eardwulf
wars.what: Three kings killed and two driven out in eight years: Ælfwald murdered (788), Osred tonsured (790) and killed (792), Ælfwald's sons drowned (791), Æthelred cut down at Corbridge (18 April 796), Osbald king for 27 days.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: No fleets and no sieges: York's strand stays open. But a merchant's host may be dead or in exile by his next visit, and in 796 King Charles, angry at the murder, takes back the gifts he had ready for the Northumbrian churches and calls the people worse than heathens: a Frankish or Frisian hull is not sure of a welcome that year.

wars.who: King Eardwulf against Wada and the men who had killed Æthelred
wars.what: A battle in Lent, on 2 April, at Billington Moor by Whalley; many fall on both sides; Wada flees.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Fought far inland, west of the hills. The king is safe on his seat after it: York is steadier for eight years.

wars.who: Eardwulf of Northumbria against Cenwulf of Mercia
wars.what: Eardwulf marches on Mercia because Cenwulf shelters his enemies; a long campaign; the bishops and great men make peace and the kings swear it on the Gospels.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Humber and the Trent mouth are a border at war for a season: goods bound between York and the Mercian markets wait.

wars.who: Eardwulf against Ælfwald II; behind them the emperor Charles and Pope Leo for Eardwulf, and (it seems) Cenwulf of Mercia and Archbishop Eanbald against
wars.what: Eardwulf is driven out, crosses to the emperor at Nijmegen in Lent 808, goes on to Rome, and is led home by a papal deacon and two Frankish abbots.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The crossing from York to the Rhine mouth carries a king and envoys: passengers of rank, and Frankish favour for whoever helped. On the way back the pope's envoy is taken by pirates in the Channel and ransomed (809).

wars.who: Ecgberht of Wessex and King Eanred
wars.what: Having taken Mercia, Ecgberht leads an army to Dore on the Northumbrian border; the Northumbrians meet him there and offer obedience, and both go home. A later writer adds plunder and tribute (?).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Nothing is burned. For a year or two a West Saxon king is overlord from the Channel to the Forth, and one king's word runs at Hamwic, Lundenwic and York.

wars.who: Rædwulf against Æthelred II; then heathen raiders
wars.what: Rædwulf drives out the king, is hastily crowned, and falls the same year fighting heathen men, with an ealdorman and much of his host. Æthelred comes back.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The first raiders on this coast for forty years, and they kill a king: the Tyne and the Humber are not safe that summer. Brass stycas with Rædwulf's name are struck and spent.

wars.who: Ælla against Osberht
wars.what: The Northumbrians throw out Osberht and take Ælla, who is not of the royal kin; the two fight until the great army is already inside York. Both strip Saint Cuthbert of estates.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A kingdom with two kings and no one to answer for a merchant's safety or his debts. The mint at York has stopped: nothing new is struck after about 855, and the old brass passes by the handful.

wars.who: the great heathen army (Ivar, Halfdan and others) against the Northumbrians
wars.what: The army rides from East Anglia, crosses the Humber and takes York on All Saints' Day, 1 November 866. On 21 March 867 Osberht and Ælla break into the city; both are killed inside the walls with eight ealdormen, and the rest make peace. The army harries to the mouth of the Tyne and sets Ecgberht over the land.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: York changes masters for ninety years. The English trading place by the Foss is given up about now (?); the minster's school and books are scattered. For some years York is a camp, and what is sold there is plunder and captives.
wars.source: ASC (A) 867; HR 867; LDE ii.6; Asser 27; Kemp 1996 (the Fishergate dig)

wars.who: the Northumbrians against the army's king Ecgberht and Archbishop Wulfhere; the great army
wars.what: The Northumbrians drive out Ecgberht and the archbishop, who flee to Burgred of Mercia. The army comes north from London, winters at Torksey on the Trent, and the old order is put back: Ricsige king, Wulfhere in his see.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The army sits a winter at Torksey, where the Trent road meets the Humber: its camp is a market for loot, slaves and silver by weight, and a bad place to pass without leave.

wars.who: Halfdan and his part of the army; the Picts and the Strathclyde Britons
wars.what: Halfdan takes winter quarters on the Tyne (874-875), overruns the land and raids the Picts and the Britons of Strathclyde. In 876 he shares out the land of the Northumbrians. In 877 he is driven out and dies in Ireland.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The monasteries of the Tyne and Wear end here, and Lindisfarne is left empty. From 876 the army are farmers in Yorkshire, 'their harrowers and plowers': they have corn, wool and hides to sell and want what a Dane wants. Silver goes by weight, not by tale.
wars.source: ASC (A) 875, 876 (the words are Ingram 1823); LDE ii.6; HSC 12; AU 877

wars.who: the Danes of Northumbria and East Anglia against King Alfred
wars.what: In 893 the Northumbrian and East Anglian Danes break their oaths, send ships round to the Devon coast and feed the armies in the south; Sigeferth comes out of Northumbria with a fleet and harries twice. In 896 their raiding ships trouble the south coast until Alfred's new long ships catch them.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A ship out of the Humber is taken for a raider in the south; a southern ship in the Humber is among the raiders' kin. Ealdorman Æthelnoth rides to York to treat with them (894).

wars.who: Æthelwold, King Alfred's nephew, with the Northumbrian army, against Edward the Elder
wars.what: Refused the West Saxon throne, Æthelwold rides by night to the army in Northumbria, which takes him as king. He comes south by sea to Essex in 901-902, raises the East Anglian Danes, and is killed at the Holme.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: York strikes a penny in an English prince's name. A fleet goes out of the Humber and does not come back.

wars.who: Edward the Elder and the Mercians against the northern army
wars.what: In 909 a West Saxon and Mercian army harries the northern army's land for five weeks, taking men and cattle. In 910 the Northumbrian Danes break the peace and raid Mercia to the Avon; coming home heavy with plunder they are caught at Tettenhall on 5 August and three kings and many holds and jarls are killed.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: York loses its kings and its fighting men in a day. The pennies of the next years name no king, only Saint Peter: the archbishop and the townsmen keep the market.

wars.who: Ragnall, grandson of Ivar, against Ealdred of Bamburgh and Constantine of the Scots; then Edward the Elder
wars.what: Ragnall comes from the Irish Sea with a fleet, fights twice at Corbridge on the Tyne (about 914 and in 918), seizes Saint Cuthbert's lands and gives them to his men, and storms York in 919. In 920, at Bakewell, the king of Scots, Ragnall, the sons of Eadwulf and all who live in Northumbria, English, Danish and Norse, take Edward as father and lord.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The kings of York are now the kings of Dublin's kin: the road from the Irish Sea over the hills to York is one house's road, and slaves, silver and Irish goods come along it. The Tyne and the Cuthbert lands are a war ground until 920.

wars.who: Æthelstan against Guthfrith
wars.what: On Sihtric's death Æthelstan takes the kingdom of the Northumbrians, drives out Guthfrith, pulls down the Danish stronghold in York and shares out the booty found in it. On 12 July at Eamont the kings of the Scots and the Welsh and Ealdred of Bamburgh give pledges and forswear idol-worship.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: One king from the Channel to the Forth. York's mint strikes the king's penny with the town's name on it; the rules of the southern towns (buy in a port, before witnesses) now reach the Ouse.

wars.who: Æthelstan against Constantine of the Scots
wars.what: The king goes north with a land army and a fleet, stops at Saint Cuthbert's shrine at Chester-le-Street with gifts, and harries Scotland by land as far as Dunnottar and by sea as far as Caithness.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The king's fleet works up the whole east coast that summer: ships are wanted, and seized. On the way he buys Amounderness from the heathen 'with no little money of my own' and gives it to the church of York.

wars.who: Olaf Guthfrithson of Dublin, Constantine of the Scots and Owain of Strathclyde against Æthelstan and Edmund
wars.what: The great fight at Brunanburh: five kings and seven jarls dead on the northern side; Olaf escapes to Dublin by ship with few men.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Dublin fleet is broken for two years and York stays the English king's.

wars.who: Olaf Guthfrithson, then Olaf Sihtricson and Ragnall Guthfrithson, against King Edmund
wars.what: On Æthelstan's death the Northumbrians take Olaf of Dublin as king. In 940 he raids to Northampton and storms Tamworth; at Leicester the two archbishops, Oda and Wulfstan, make a peace that gives him all the land north of Watling Street. He dies in 941; the men of York harry Lindisfarne. Edmund wins back the Five Boroughs in 942, stands godfather to Olaf Sihtricson in 943, and in 944 drives both kings out.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: For five years York and Dublin are one kingdom again and its pennies carry a raven and a Norse word for king. Lincoln and the Trent towns change hands twice; the Humber is the Dublin kings' water until 944.

wars.who: King Edmund against the Britons of Strathclyde
wars.what: Edmund harries all Cumbria and lets it to Malcolm of the Scots on condition that he be his helper by land and sea.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The western end of the York to Dublin road is put under a friendly king.

wars.who: King Eadred against the Northumbrians and their kings Eric and Olaf
wars.what: The Northumbrians swear to Eadred at Tanshelf (947) and take Eric. In 948 Eadred harries the land and Wilfrid's minster at Ripon is burned; the army in York falls on his rearguard at Castleford; he threatens to turn back and destroy the land, and they give Eric up and pay. Olaf rules 949 to 952, Eric again 952 to 954, when he is driven out and killed on Stainmore.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Four changes of king in seven years, each with its own penny. A merchant's safe-conduct dies with the king who gave it. After 954 York is an English town for good, and richer for it.

wars.who: Thored son of Gunnar against Westmorland
wars.what: Thored harries Westmorland, perhaps on the king's order against the Cumbrians (?).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A raid over the hills; nothing at sea.
wars.source: ASC (D/E) 966 (the words 'Thored, the son of Gunner, plundered Westmorland' are Ingram 1823)

wars.who: King Æthelred against the Cumbrians and the Isle of Man
wars.what: The king harries almost all Cumbria; his fleet, sent round by Chester to meet him, cannot, and harries Man instead.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Irish Sea side is shut for a summer. The Danish fleet has gone to Normandy that year, so the east coast is quiet.

wars.who: Malcolm II of the Scots against the Northumbrians; Uhtred
wars.what: The Scots lay siege to the new town of Durham. Old Earl Waltheof stays in Bamburgh; his son Uhtred raises the men of Bernicia and Yorkshire and cuts the Scots to pieces. The best-looking heads, their hair combed, are set on stakes round the walls; four women are given a cow each for washing them. (Some would date this later (?).)
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Tyne and Wear are safe again and Durham is proved a strong place: the saint's market on the Wear grows from here.

wars.who: Sweyn Forkbeard and his son Cnut against King Æthelred and Edmund Ironside; Earl Uhtred between them
wars.what: In 1013 Sweyn brings his fleet into the Humber and up the Trent to Gainsborough; Uhtred and all Northumbria bow to him at once. Sweyn dies there on 3 February 1014. In 1016 Uhtred is harrying in the west with Edmund when Cnut marches on York; he comes home, submits, and is killed in the hall at Wiheal. Cnut makes Eric of Hlathir earl.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Humber is the Danish kings' gate into England: a fleet lies in the Trent for months and must be fed. From 1016 York, the Danish towns and Denmark are under one king for nearly thirty years, and Danish merchants are at home in York.

wars.who: Malcolm II of the Scots and Owain the Bald of Strathclyde against the Northumbrians north of the Tees
wars.what: A comet is seen for thirty nights; then the men between Tees and Tweed are almost all cut down at Carham on the Tweed. Bishop Aldhun dies of grief a few days after. The Tweed becomes the border; Lothian is the Scots' (if it was not already). The year may be 1016 (?).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Bamburgh's lords lose the land north of the Tweed and most of their fighting men. Lindisfarne and Bamburgh are now on a frontier.

wars.who: the house of Bamburgh, the house of Thurbrand, Duncan of the Scots, Siward
wars.what: Earl Ealdred is killed by Carl (about 1038). His brother Eadwulf harries the Cumbrians (1038). Duncan besieges Durham and is beaten off with great loss; the heads of his foot-soldiers are set up in the market place (1040). In 1041 Eadwulf comes to Harthacnut under safe-conduct and Siward kills him and takes all Northumbria.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Durham has a market place by 1040. After 1041 one hard earl holds everything from the Humber to the Tweed, and the roads are safer than they have been in a lifetime.

wars.who: Earl Siward against Macbeth, king of Scots
wars.what: Siward goes into Scotland with a fleet and a land army and on 27 July, the day of the Seven Sleepers, puts Macbeth to flight with great slaughter and takes such plunder as no man had before. His son Osbeorn and his sister's son Siward are killed, with some of his and the king's housecarls.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Ships are pressed from the Humber and the Tyne for the fleet. The plunder of Scotland is sold in York that autumn.

wars.who: Malcolm III of the Scots against Tostig's earldom
wars.what: While Earl Tostig is at Rome with Archbishop Ealdred, Malcolm, his sworn brother, harries Northumbria and breaks the peace of Saint Cuthbert on Lindisfarne.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The coast north of the Tyne is raided by land; Lindisfarne is no shelter that year.

wars.who: the thegns of Northumbria against Earl Tostig
wars.what: On 3 October some two hundred thegns come into York, kill Tostig's housecarls Amund and Ravenswart and, the next day, more than two hundred of his men; they break open his treasury, outlaw him, send for Morcar and march south to Northampton, harrying as they go. At Oxford on 28 October Earl Harold gives them what they ask and renews the law of Cnut. Tostig sails to Count Baldwin in Flanders.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: York is in the rebels' hands for a month and the earl's silver is in theirs. Northampton's country is stripped of cattle and of men, hundreds of whom are driven north. Tostig, in Flanders with ships and a grudge, is next year's raider.

wars.who: Tostig and Harald Hardrada of Norway against Earls Edwin and Morcar, then King Harold
wars.what: In May Tostig comes into the Humber with sixty ships and harries Lindsey; the earls drive him off and he flees to Scotland with twelve small ships. In September Harald of Norway comes with three hundred ships, burns Scarborough (the saga says), sails up the Ouse to Riccall, beats the earls at Fulford on 20 September and takes hostages from York. On 25 September King Harold falls on them at Stamford Bridge; both are killed; twenty-four ships take the rest home.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Every ship in the Humber and Ouse in September is taken, burned or pressed. The men of York lose a great part of their fighting men at Fulford, a week before they are needed again.
wars.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1066; JW 1066; Snorri, Heimskringla: Haralds saga Sigurðarsonar

wars.who: King William against the Northumbrians, Edgar Ætheling and the fleet of Sweyn Estrithson of Denmark
wars.what: 1068: the north rises; William builds a castle at York. 28 January 1069: Robert de Comines and his men are killed at Durham; the castle at York is attacked; William relieves it and builds a second. September 1069: a Danish fleet of 240 ships under Sweyn's sons and brother comes into the Humber; the garrison fires the houses near the castles and the fire takes the city and the minster (19 September); on 21 September the Danes and the English storm both castles. William buys the Danes off, keeps Christmas at York, and through the winter lays the land waste from the Humber to the Tyne. The Danes leave in the summer of 1070.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The end of the old York. The city is burned, the land between York and Durham is said to lie empty for nine years, the people sell themselves into bondage for bread. In 1086 the king's book still calls most of Yorkshire waste. The game's span ends before this; it is here so the last years read true.
wars.source: ASC (D/E) 1068, 1069, 1070; JW 1069; HR 1069, 1070; Orderic Vitalis iv; DB

raids.who: heathen men from the north, by ship
raids.what: The church of Saint Cuthbert is plundered: altars dug up, treasures taken, some brothers killed, some carried off in fetters, some driven out naked, some drowned in the sea. The community stays.
raids.source: ASC (D/E) 793; HR 793; LDE ii.5; Alcuin ep. 16, 20

raids.who: heathen men, by ship
raids.what: They plunder King Ecgfrith's monastery at the mouth of the Don. One of their leaders is killed there; a storm breaks their ships; many drown, and those who reach the shore alive are killed at the river mouth.

raids.who: heathen men, by ship
raids.what: The churches of Hartness (by Hartlepool) and Tynemouth are plundered and the raiders go home with the spoil. Told only by a late writer.

raids.who: heathen men
raids.what: King Rædwulf, newly crowned, fights them and is killed with Ealdorman Alfred and a great part of his men.

raids.who: the great heathen army under Ivar and Halfdan
raids.what: The army comes from East Anglia over the Humber and takes the city on All Saints' Day, while the Northumbrians are at war among themselves. The walls are old Roman work and not kept up.
raids.source: ASC (A) 867 ('over the mouth of the Humber to the Northumbrians, as far as York', Ingram 1823); LDE ii.6; Asser 27

raids.who: the great heathen army; Kings Osberht and Ælla
raids.what: The two kings break in; some of their men are killed inside the walls and some outside, both kings among them. The army then harries north to the mouth of the Tyne.

raids.who: the great heathen army (?)
raids.what: Hild's house on the cliff is said to have been destroyed by Ivar and Ubba and to have lain empty for two hundred years. No writer of the time says so; the digging shows the house ending in the ninth century.
raids.source: William of Malmesbury, Gesta pontificum iii.116; the Whitby 'Memorial of benefactions' (12th century) (?)

raids.who: Halfdan's army, wintering on the Tyne
raids.what: The army lies on the Tyne through the winter of 874-875 and wastes the country round. The houses of Jarrow, Wearmouth and Tynemouth are not heard of again as living monasteries until after 1070.

raids.who: Halfdan's army (feared, not seen)
raids.what: Bishop Eardulf and Abbot Eadred take up Saint Cuthbert's body, Saint Oswald's head, Aidan's bones and the great gospel book, and leave the island before the army comes. They wander seven years.

raids.where: the coasts of Wessex (out of Northumbria)
raids.who: the Danes of Northumbria and East Anglia; Sigeferth with a fleet
raids.what: A hundred ships go round to besiege Exeter and a fort on the north Devon coast; Sigeferth harries the coast twice and sails home.

raids.who: Ragnall, grandson of Ivar, with a fleet from the Irish Sea
raids.what: Ragnall lands on the Tyne (first about 914), beats Ealdred of Bamburgh and the Scots, and shares out Saint Cuthbert's estates from Eden to the Wear between his men Scula and Onlafbald. Onlafbald mocks the saint at the church door at Chester-le-Street, swearing by his gods Thor and Odin, and falls dead on the threshold.

raids.who: the men of York, under Olaf Sihtricson (?)
raids.what: After Olaf Guthfrithson burns Tyninghame and dies, the men of York lay Lindisfarne waste and kill many.

raids.who: King Eadred's army
raids.what: Eadred harries all Northumbria because they had taken Eric for their king, and the minster that Saint Wilfrid built at Ripon is burned. Wilfrid's bones are taken south to Canterbury.
raids.source: ASC (D) 948 ('because they had taken Eric for their king', Ingram 1823)

raids.who: a fleet of the Danes (the fleet that had fought at Maldon)
raids.what: Bamburgh is broken into and much plunder taken. The fleet then comes to the mouth of the Humber and does great harm in Lindsey and in Northumbria. A great English army is raised, and its leaders Fræna, Godwine and Frithegist are the first to run.

raids.who: Malcolm II of the Scots
raids.what: The Scots besiege Durham and are destroyed by Uhtred (see wars).

raids.who: Duncan, king of Scots
raids.what: Duncan besieges Durham with a great host and is beaten off; his horsemen are cut down and the heads of his foot-soldiers are hung on stakes in the market place.

raids.who: Malcolm III of the Scots
raids.what: Malcolm harries his sworn brother Tostig's earldom while the earl is at Rome, and breaks Saint Cuthbert's peace on the island.

raids.who: the thegns of Northumbria, led by Gamelbearn, Dunstan son of Æthelnoth and Glonieorn son of Heardwulf
raids.what: They enter York with two hundred men, catch Tostig's Danish housecarls Amund and Ravenswart in flight and kill them outside the walls; next day they kill more than two hundred of his household on the north bank, break open his treasury and carry off his weapons, gold and silver.

raids.who: Tostig, with sixty ships from Flanders and the south coast
raids.what: Tostig comes into the Humber in May and harries in Lindsey, killing many good men. Earls Edwin and Morcar drive him out; his shipmen desert him and he reaches Scotland with twelve small ships.

raids.who: Harald Hardrada of Norway and Tostig, with three hundred ships
raids.what: They burn Scarborough and harry Holderness (the saga), sail up the Ouse and leave the ships at Riccall. On 20 September, the eve of Saint Matthew, they beat Edwin and Morcar at Fulford, two miles below York; many English are drowned in the river and the ditches. York gives hostages and food and agrees to march south with them. Five days later they are dead at Stamford Bridge.
raids.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1066; JW 1066; Snorri, Heimskringla: Haralds saga Sigurðarsonar (Scarborough only there (?))

raids.who: the Northumbrians beyond the Tees
raids.what: They break in at the gates at first light and kill King William's earl Robert de Comines and his men through the streets; the house he lies in is burned.

raids.who: the fleet of Sweyn Estrithson (240 ships, under his sons Harald and Cnut and his brother Osbeorn) with Edgar Ætheling, Waltheof and Gospatric
raids.what: The fleet comes into the Humber after trying Dover, Sandwich, Ipswich and Norwich. On Saturday 19 September the Norman garrison fires the houses by the castles; the fire takes the whole city and Saint Peter's minster. On Monday the Danes and English storm both castles, kill the garrison (more than three thousand, it is said), break the castles down and go back to their ships with the plunder.

raids.who: King William's army
raids.what: Through the winter of 1069-1070 the king wastes the land from the Humber to the Tees and then to the Tyne, burning houses, corn, cattle and tools. The church of Saint Paul at Jarrow is burned (?). The bishop and his people flee from Durham to Lindisfarne with Saint Cuthbert's body (11 December) and come back in Lent.
raids.source: HR 1069; LDE iii.15; Orderic Vitalis iv; ASC (D) 1069

raids.who: Malcolm III of the Scots
raids.what: Malcolm comes through Cumbria into Teesdale, harries Cleveland and Hartness and watches Saint Peter's church at Wearmouth burn. At Wearmouth he finds Edgar Ætheling and his sisters waiting in their ships for a wind to Scotland. His men drive off so many captives that there was no village in Scotland, it was said, without an English slave.

laws.what: The pope's legates George of Ostia and Theophylact of Todi hold a council in Northumbria with King Ælfwald and Archbishop Eanbald and read out twenty decrees. Among them: kings are to be lawfully chosen and no one is to plot a king's death; tithes are to be paid; no usury; just and equal measures and weights for all; heathen ways are to stop (cutting horses' noses and tails, eating horse, casting lots to settle suits).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: One measure and one weight for buyer and seller is church law here from 786, and lending at interest is a sin a priest can name. Do not offer horse-flesh. The decree against killing kings is broken within two years.
laws.source: the legates' report, Alcuin ep. 3 (MGH Epp. IV), c. 12, 17, 19; ASC (D/E) 785 (=786)

laws.what: Sanctuary at the minster: the sons of King Ælfwald are in York minster under the church's peace, and King Æthelred has them drawn out by false promises and drowned at Wonwaldremere.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The church's peace is the only shelter there is, and it holds only while the king fears God. A debtor or a man with blood on him can reach an altar; he cannot count on staying alive if he is talked out of it.

laws.what: Halfdan shares out the land of the Northumbrians among his army. From now the law south of the Tees is the settlers' custom: the land is counted in three ridings and in wapentakes, the great men are jarls and holds, and money is reckoned in marks and ores (a mark is eight ores; an ore is sixteen pennies in later reckoning).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A bargain at York is struck before the men of a wapentake, with weapons shaken for assent, and a fine is named in ores. Silver is weighed and tested with a knife point until the York mint opens again about 895: bring scales and expect your coin to be nicked.
laws.source: ASC (A) 876; DB (ridings, wapentakes, the ore); the hoards (num.)

laws.what: Guthred's peace. The Danish army and the English swear peace and faith over Saint Cuthbert's body on Oswigesdune. The king gives the saint all the land between the Tyne and the Wear, and grants that whoever flees to the saint's body shall have peace for thirty-seven days and nights, and that breaking that peace costs what breaking the king's peace costs. King Alfred is said to have confirmed it.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Between Tyne and Wear the lord is a dead saint and his bishop: dues are paid to them at Chester-le-Street, and a man in trouble can buy five weeks there to find his oath-helpers or his silver.

laws.what: King Æthelstan's law reaches York (the Grately decrees, about 926-930): one coinage over all the king's land, struck only in a port (a market town); no one is to buy goods worth more than twenty pence outside a port, but in it, before the port-reeve or another trusty man; a moneyer who strikes false coin loses the hand he did it with, and it is set up over the mint.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: At York from 927: sell and buy inside the town before witnesses, and change foreign silver at the mint for the king's penny with EFORWIC on it. How far the law bit among the Danes of York is another matter (?).
laws.source: Laws, II Æthelstan 12-14; num.: Æthelstan's York pennies (Blunt 1974)

laws.what: King Edgar's decree after the great plague (IV Edgar; 962-963, or some years later (?)): the Danes are to keep their own law, as good as they can best choose; but one rule is for all, English, Danes and Britons: every sale is to be made before sworn witnesses, thirty-six chosen for each borough and twelve for each small borough or wapentake; a man who rides out to buy must tell his neighbours first and name his witnesses when he comes home. Earl Oslac and all the army in his earldom are to see it kept.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: At York two or three of the thirty-six must see every bargain. Goods bought without witness are taken for stolen: the buyer loses them and may lose his neck. A stranger does well to buy through a host who knows the witnesses.

laws.what: Edgar's new money: one design of penny for all England, the old called in, the moneyer and the town named on every coin; the type is changed every few years after.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: After each change the old penny is not good money in the market: take it, and any foreign silver, to a York moneyer and lose a part in the changing. The king's profit is in that part.
laws.source: num.: Dolley and Metcalf 1961; Naismith, MEC 8

laws.what: King Æthelred's law for the Danish boroughs, made at Wantage (III Æthelred, about 997; written for the Five Boroughs south of the Humber, and the same custom shows at York in 1066): breach of the peace given in the court of the Five Boroughs costs twelve hundreds of silver, in one borough six, in a wapentake one, and in an ale-house six half-marks if a man is killed and twelve ores if he lives. Twelve leading thegns swear on relics to accuse no innocent man. No one is to slaughter a beast without two witnesses and keeps the hide and head three nights. A moneyer who works in a wood or any such place forfeits his life.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A crew's brawl in a York ale-house has a price in ores before it has a judge. A 'hundred' of silver is eight pounds. Coin from a man who strikes in the woods will hang you both.

laws.what: Archbishop Wulfstan of York (1002-1023) writes down how ranks stood 'once': a ceorl who throve to five hides, a church, a kitchen, a bell-house and a seat in the king's hall was worth a thegn's rights; and 'if a merchant thrived, so that he fared thrice over the wide sea by his own means, then was he thenceforth of thane-right worthy.' With it, the north people's law of man-prices in thrymsas: the king 30,000; an archbishop or ætheling 15,000; a bishop or ealdorman 8,000; a hold or a king's high-reeve 4,000; a thegn, of church or world, 2,000; a ceorl 266.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Three crossings in your own ship with your own goods and you may claim a thegn's standing: a thegn's oath, a thegn's man-price. And you know what a killing costs in the north, by the dead man's rank.
laws.source: Laws, 'Of people's ranks and law' 6 (Thorpe 1840, quoted) and 'North people's law' (Thorpe 1840)

laws.what: The army-tax (heregeld), first raised in 1012 to pay Thorkell's forty-five ships and taken every year until King Edward ends it in 1051. The north is lightly taxed beside the south; Earl Tostig's attempt to raise more is one cause of 1065.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Silver leaves the land every year for the fleet's pay, and comes back through the shipmen's hands in the ports. In a tax month men sell cheap for coin.

laws.what: At Oxford the Danes and the English agree to keep King Edgar's law. In the north this means what it meant under Edgar: the Danes' own custom, under an earl of the king's choosing.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: No new rules, and that is the news: Cnut's peace keeps the old market law, the witnesses and the York mint.

laws.what: Cnut's great law-book, given at Winchester at Christmas (1020 or 1021) and written by Archbishop Wulfstan of York: one coinage, and no one may refuse good money; weights and measures to be made right; Christian men are not to be sold out of the land, least of all to heathens; nothing worth over four pence, alive or dead, is to be bought without four true witnesses, in town or country; among the Danes a fine is 'law-slit' and the king keeps his own pleas there (fighting, breach of his peace, house-breaking, neglect of the levy).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The slave trade to Dublin and beyond is against the king's law from now, though not ended. A sale over four pence needs four witnesses. A York penny must be taken at its face anywhere in England.

laws.what: The Northumbrian Priests' Law, from Archbishop Wulfstan's circle at York (about 1008 to soon after 1023): Sunday trading is forbidden everywhere, with every folk-meeting and all carrying by wagon, horse or back, on pain of twelve ores for a free man and a flogging for a slave; travellers may carry food at need, and for fear of war a man may travel on a feast-eve between York and six miles out. Heathen worship, sacrifice, soothsaying and witchcraft cost a king's thegn ten half-marks, a landholder six, a lesser man twelve ores; an enclosure of peace round a stone, a tree or a well is fined. Rome-penny is due by Saint Peter's day. A man has one wife.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: No market on Sunday in York and no loading. The fines tell you what your Danish neighbours still do at a tree or a well, and that you should not be seen at it.

laws.what: King Cnut writes home from Rome that the emperor and the king of Burgundy have promised that his people, English and Danes, merchants and pilgrims, shall go to Rome and back in firm peace, free of the many barriers and unjust tolls.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A merchant of York on the Rhine and Alpine roads can name Cnut's letter at a toll-bar. Whether the toll-man has heard of it is his own affair.
laws.source: Cnut's letter of 1027, in JW 1031 and WM GR ii.183

laws.what: At Oxford on 28 October, to end the northern rising, Earl Harold on the king's behalf renews the law of Cnut for the Northumbrians and confirms Morcar as their earl.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Tostig's new taxes and his rough justice are undone: dues at York go back to what they were in Cnut's day.

laws.what: The customs of York in King Edward's day, as written down in 1086. The city has seven shires, one of them the archbishop's, where he has the full custom. Peace given by the king's hand or seal, if broken, is paid for to the king alone with twelve hundreds, each of eight pounds; peace given by the earl with six. A man outlawed by law can be given peace only by the king. The king has three roads by land and a fourth by water, and every offence on them is his and the earl's, whoever's land they cross. Four lawmen hold their privilege for life by the king's writ. The burgesses of York pay no death-due. The city pays the king fifty-three pounds a year (?).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The Ouse is the king's road: a wrong done to you on the river is the king's business and costs the doer dear. Pay the archbishop's toll in his shire and the king's and earl's in the other six. For real safety, get the king's peace by hand or seal: ninety-six pounds stand behind it.
laws.source: DB (Yorkshire, folio 298; the figures not re-checked (?))

coins.what: Small thick pennies of poor silver, the first of the kind later called stycas (a styca is 'a piece'). Æthelred I's name on one side, the moneyer's on the other: Ceolbald, Cuthheard, Hnifula, Tidwulf; one kind shows a shrine. Eardwulf's coins, by Cuthheard, are very rare (the first was found in 1994) and Ælfwald II's the same. South of the Humber and in Francia everyone now strikes the broad thin penny: these do not match it and do not travel.
coins.source: num.: Pirie 1996, Coins of the Kingdom of Northumbria; Naismith, MEC 8

coins.what: Eanred's stycas, the silver falling year by year until they are pale brass by the 830s; many moneyers (Cuthheard, Eadwine, Herreth, Wilheah, Dægberht and more (?)). Archbishop Eanbald II strikes his own with his own moneyers. One broad silver penny in Eanred's name, of southern make, is known; whether it is this Eanred's is argued (?).

Brass stycas in huge numbers: Æthelred II (moneyers Eardwulf, Fordred, Leofthegn, Monne, Wendelberht), Rædwulf (844), Osberht (Eanwulf, Monne, Winiberht), Archbishops Wigmund (Coenred, Æthelweard, Hunlaf) and Wulfhere (Wulfred). No silver to speak of. Many are clumsy copies. A bronze bucket of about eight thousand was buried in Hexham churchyard and found in 1832.

One gold piece of Archbishop Wigmund: his facing bust and name, and on the back MVNVS DIVINVM, 'the gift of God', copied from a gold coin of the emperor Louis the Pious. A gift-piece for an altar or a great man, not market money. One is known.

No coin is struck in Northumbria. Until 867 the old brass still passes. Under the army, silver goes by weight: cut pieces of arm-rings and brooches, bars, Frankish and southern English pennies, and dirhams from the east, all nicked with a knife to try the metal.
coins.source: num.: the hoards of the Danish north (Williams 2009); Blackburn 2004

coins.what: York's mint opens again with good silver pennies and halfpennies in the names of Siefred and Cnut, the letters set in the shape of a cross. They read EBRAICE CIVITAS (the city of York), CVNNETTI (unexplained), and church words: MIRABILIA FECIT ('he has done wonders', from the psalm), DNS DS REX ('the Lord God is king'). A few name ALVALDVS (Æthelwold). About three thousand lay in the Cuerdale hoard, buried by the Ribble about 905-910 with some forty kilos of silver: more than eight thousand pieces in all, with hack-silver, bars and dirhams.
coins.source: num.: Blackburn 2004, 'The coinage of Scandinavian York'; the Cuerdale hoard (found 1840; British Museum)

coins.what: The Saint Peter penny: no king's name, only SCI PETRI MO, 'Saint Peter's money', and the city's. Lighter and rougher as the years go.

Ragnall's pennies (RAIENALT), with a bow and arrow, a hand, and a hammer. Then Saint Peter's money again, now with a sword laid across it and Thor's hammer beside the cross on the same coin. Sihtric's sword pennies (SITRIC REX) are struck for him south of the Humber. The Vale of York hoard, hidden about 927-928 near Harrogate, shows what a rich man held that year: 617 coins in a Frankish silver-gilt cup with a gold arm-ring, bars and cut silver; Saint Peter sword pennies, Æthelstan's newest type, Frankish deniers, and dirhams from as far as Samarkand.
coins.source: num.: Blackburn 2004; the Vale of York hoard (found 2007; British Museum and Yorkshire Museum)

coins.what: King Æthelstan's pennies struck at York, first with a church or tower, then with his title REX TO BRIT, 'king of all Britain', and the town's name in English, EFORWIC. One moneyer, Regnald, strikes nearly all of them. An iron die for a Saint Peter sword penny and lead trial strikings of Æthelstan's dies were found in the workshops at Coppergate.
coins.source: num.: Blunt 1974, 'The coinage of Athelstan'; Hall 1984 (Coppergate); Laws, II Æthelstan 14

coins.what: A new penny with every king. Olaf Guthfrithson: a raven with spread wings and ANLAF CVNVNC, 'King Olaf' in Norse, among the first Norse words written in Latin letters. Olaf Sihtricson, Ragnall and a Sihtric: a three-cornered knot and a war-banner (moneyers Farman, Ascolv (?)). Edmund and Eadred between them, in the English style. Eric: ERIC REX, the second time with a sword (moneyers Ingelgar and Radulf); about thirty of his coins are known.
coins.source: num.: Blackburn 2004; Blunt, Stewart and Lyon 1989, Coinage in Tenth-Century England

coins.what: English pennies of Eadred, Eadwig and Edgar struck at York in the northern style, the moneyer's name in two lines; the town is not always named.

The reformed penny: the king's head, the moneyer and EOFER or EOFR on every coin, the type called in and changed every six years and later every two or three. York is one of the four great mints with London, Lincoln and Winchester, with ten to twenty moneyers at work at once, and most of them have Norse names: Arngrim, Arncetel, Iocetel, Othgrim, Scula, Styrcol, Thorr, Ulfcetel (?). Sums are still told in marks and ores. Much of this silver goes to Denmark as tribute and pay, and turns up in Scandinavian hoards.
coins.source: num.: Dolley and Metcalf 1961; Naismith, MEC 8; Smart 1986 (the moneyers' names)

coins.what: Harold's one type, with PAX across the back, is struck at York in 1066; King William's first types follow from the same moneyers. The mint goes on through the burning of the city.
coins.source: num.: North, English Hammered Coinage i

church.what: Archbishop Ælberht, having rebuilt York's school and gathered its library, gives the books to his pupil Alcuin and the see to Eanbald, and dies on 8 November. A new church of the Holy Wisdom with thirty altars is hallowed days before. Alcuin leaves for King Charles's court about 782.
church.source: Alcuin, poem on the bishops, kings and saints of York, lines 1507-1562; HR 780

church.what: Lindisfarne plundered on 8 June. Alcuin writes from Francia to the king, to Bishop Higbald and to the monks of Wearmouth and Jarrow: the saint did not defend his own; look to your ways, your dress, your feasting.

Archbishop Eanbald I dies on 10 August; Eanbald II is hallowed at Sockburn on the 14th and gets the pallium on 8 September 797. He strikes coin in his own name and keeps a large armed following, for which Alcuin scolds him.
Alcuin of York dies at Tours on 19 May. The books he asked to have sent from York to Francia stay a traded thing between the two schools.

Bishop Ecgred of Lindisfarne (830-845) builds a church at Norham on the Tweed, moves Aidan's old timber church there from the island with the body of King Ceolwulf, and gives the saint Jedburgh, Gainford on the Tees and other estates. The see's weight shifts to the mainland a generation before the army comes.
Wulfhere becomes archbishop of York and Eardulf bishop of Lindisfarne: the two men who will carry their churches through the army's coming. Wulfhere strikes the last of the archbishops' brass stycas.
York falls. The archbishop stays and makes his peace with the army; the school and the library of Ælberht and Alcuin are not heard of again. The army wastes the churches as far as the Tyne mouth.

Archbishop Wulfhere is driven out with King Ecgberht by the Northumbrians and shelters with King Burgred in Mercia; he is put back in 873 and holds the see under Danish kings until his death (892 or 900). The see is then empty for some years.

Bishop Eardulf and Abbot Eadred leave Lindisfarne with Saint Cuthbert's body and wander seven years with seven bearers and a cart. They try to cross to Ireland from the mouth of the Derwent; a storm turns them back and the gospel book goes overboard, and is found unharmed on the sands at Whithorn at a low tide.

After four months at Crayke the community settles at Chester-le-Street. King Guthred gives it the land between Tyne and Wear and the right of sanctuary. The bishops of Saint Cuthbert sit there for 112 years.

Guthred, a Danish king, is buried in York minster. From about this year York's pennies carry crosses and psalm words, and from about 905 Saint Peter's name alone: the archbishop has a hand in the mint.

Ragnall's man Onlafbald, given Saint Cuthbert's land, comes into the church at Chester-le-Street before Bishop Cutheard, swears by Thor and Odin to be the saint's enemy, and drops dead at the door. The story is the community's own; the heathen lords on its land are real.

King Æthelstan, marching north, stops at Chester-le-Street and gives the saint a gospel book, a Life of Cuthbert, vestments, plate, bells and the estate of Wearmouth. On 7 June at Nottingham he gives the church of York the whole of Amounderness, which he has bought from the heathen.

Archbishop Wulfstan I (931-956) leads the Northumbrian council in swearing to King Eadred at Tanshelf, and then in taking Eric. He had gone south with Olaf's army in 940 and made the peace at Leicester.
Ripon minster, Saint Wilfrid's church, is burned by Eadred's army. Canterbury afterwards said it had carried Wilfrid's bones south.

King Eadred has Archbishop Wulfstan shut up in the stronghold of Iudanburh, because he had often been accused to the king. He is freed in 954 and given back a bishop's rank at Dorchester, not at York; he dies in 956.

From now the archbishops are the king's men from south of the Humber, often of Danish blood, and often hold a rich southern see as well: Oscytel (about 958-971), Oswald (971-992, with Worcester), Ealdwulf (995-1002), Wulfstan II (1002-1023).
church.source: ASC (B) 971; Byrhtferth, Life of Saint Oswald

church.what: Bishop Aldhun, warned of raiders, takes Saint Cuthbert's body from Chester-le-Street to Ripon and, months later, to the wooded rock of Durham in a loop of the Wear, where the cart will go no further. Uhtred, the earl's son, brings the whole people from the Coquet to the Tees to clear it. The stone church is hallowed on 4 September 998.

A monk of Ramsey writes that York is crowded and rich with the goods of merchants who come from everywhere, above all from the Danish people; he counts thirty thousand grown people, which is too many, and says the walls are old and broken.
church.source: Byrhtferth, Life of Saint Oswald v.3

church.what: Archbishop Wulfstan II preaches his 'Sermon of the Wolf to the English': the land is ruined for its sins, kin sells kin to strangers, slaves run off to the raiders. He writes the laws of Æthelred and of Cnut.

Elfred son of Westou, sacrist of Durham, who goes every year to pray at Jarrow on Bede's day, comes home alone one year and never goes again: Bede's bones are in a linen bag in Saint Cuthbert's coffin. The year is about 1022 (?).
King Cnut walks five miles barefoot from Garmondsway to Saint Cuthbert's tomb at Durham and gives the saint Staindrop and its villages.

Earl Siward is buried at Galmanho, outside York's walls, in the church he built and had hallowed to God and Olaf, a Norwegian king twenty-five years dead. In these years Orm son of Gamal buys the ruined minster of Saint Gregory at Kirkdale and builds it new 'in the days of Edward the king and Tosti the earl', and has it cut on a sundial over the door.
church.source: ASC (C/D) 1055; the Kirkdale sundial (the stone itself)

church.what: Ealdred, bishop of Worcester, is made archbishop of York and goes to Rome for the pallium with Earl Tostig. The pope refuses him, robbers strip the party outside Rome, and the pope gives way. Ealdred builds at Beverley and York and crowns King William on Christmas Day 1066.

Archbishop Ealdred dies on 11 September as the Danish fleet comes in. Eight days later Saint Peter's minster burns with the city. In December the bishop of Durham flees with Saint Cuthbert's body to Lindisfarne; the tide, which should have barred them, is out, and closes behind them.
Thomas of Bayeux, a Norman, is made archbishop of York and finds the minster a burnt shell with three of its seven canons left. Malcolm of the Scots burns Saint Peter's at Wearmouth.
church.source: Hugh the Chanter, History of the Church of York; HR 1070
